title: Taken up (Assumption, 15 August)
hookLine: defined in 1950, Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (CCC 966)
last: A SWORD SHALL PIERCE THY SOUL.

cards: In much of Europe, mid-August is when everything closes. In Italy it's called Ferragosto: shops shut, cities empty, families head to the beach.
In France, Spain, Poland and plenty of other places, August fifteenth is a public holiday, and most tourists have no idea why.
Ferragosto's name goes back to the Roman emperor Augustus, but the day itself is a feast of Mary, one of the oldest. Scripture doesn't tell us how Mary's life on earth ended.
So where does the feast come from, and why did a pope in 1950 make it a formal teaching of the faith?

teach.b: On November first, 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it: Mary, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.
First he wrote to bishops all over the world asking what their people believed. The answer was overwhelming. Christians had been celebrating this in some form for well over a thousand years.
Jesus ascended: he went up by his own power. Mary was assumed, from the Latin for taken up. She didn't rise by herself; she was received.
And notice what the definition leaves out: whether Mary died first. Most Catholics, and the long tradition, say she did.
Eastern Christians call the same August feast the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary.
Catholics often point to a picture from the Book of Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars."
But the Church is honest that the teaching rests on tradition and the Church's faith, not one verse.
The Catechism calls it a share in her son's resurrection and a preview of ours. In the Creed, Catholics say they believe in the resurrection of the body.

Not escape from the body: the body, raised. The Assumption says that what God did for Jesus, he's already begun doing for one of us. In that view, your body, with its knees and scars and tiredness, isn't a shell.
Catholics say it's part of you, and it's meant for glory.

how: Catholics celebrate the Assumption on 15 August, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and Eastern Christians keep the same day as the Dormition of the Mother of God.

games.q: you're Pius XII, thinking about defining the Assumption. what do you do first?
o: ask bishops worldwide what their people believe.
games.why: he wrote to bishops around the world, and the answer was overwhelmingly yes, before he defined it in 1950.

practice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face, noticing where you're tired or sore or tight without judging any of it. Thank each part for carrying you today, and let your shoulders drop.
If you pray, you can thank God for your body, as it is; if you don't, just be kind to it for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Assumption. From the Latin for taken up. Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into glory, a preview of the resurrection. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a taking up, a receiving. from assumere, to take to oneself.

carryVoice: Your line: the body matters. He ascended by his own power; she was taken up. That's day eighty-two.
